identity.journal: Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific

paper_type_evidence.quote: We report the first very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) experiment conducted in the 690 GHz atmospheric window.

The objective of this work was not only to achieve a technical milestone but also to evaluate the practical requirements—including instrumental readiness, calibration strategy, atmospheric conditions, and operational resources—necessary for sustained near-terahertz VLBI.

question.value: Evaluate the feasibility and practical requirements—including instrumental readiness, ALMA Band 9 phasing performance, calibration strategy, and atmospheric conditions—for ground-based very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) in the 690 GHz atmospheric window.

evidence.quote: The objective of this work was not only to achieve a technical milestone but also to evaluate the practical requirements—including instrumental readiness, calibration strategy, atmospheric conditions, and operational resources—necessary for sustained near-terahertz VLBI.

Our goal in this 690 GHz experiment was to demonstrate the feasibility of VLBI at such high frequencies, thereby establishing a critical stepping stone toward future observations of the supermassive black holes Sgr A* and M87*.
This paper makes use of the following ALMA data:ADS/JAO.ALMA#2011.0.00014.E.

On 2024 November 21, observations with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, the Atacama Pathfinder EXperiment (APEX), and the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope (JCMT) were carried out using ALMA’s newly developed Band 9 phasing capability.
For the primary and secondary targets, we also scheduled a Band 6 (230 GHz) session as a VLBI benchmark test of overall system, since observations in this band are well established.

claims.hypothesis: Ground-based VLBI fringe detection in the 690 GHz atmospheric window is technically feasible using the ALMA Phasing System at Band 9 in combination with submillimeter VLBI stations.
claims.experiment: Conducted a 685 GHz VLBI experiment on 2024 November 21 with phased ALMA (45 antennas), APEX, and JCMT observing quasar J0423-0120, correlating the data with DiFX and fitting fringes with HOPS.
claims.result: Detected statistically significant fringes on the ALMA-APEX baseline in Scan 2 at 691 GHz with SNR = 12.0 (X1X) and 9.7 (Y1Y) over a 60 s fringe search interval and 20 s nominal solution interval.
claims.finding: Near-terahertz ground-based VLBI at 690 GHz is technically feasible under excellent weather conditions.

evidence.quote: Fringes were detected on the ALMA–APEX baseline during a scan of the quasar J0423–0120, with a signal-to-noise ratio of ∼12 and useful fringe recovery over solution intervals of order tens of seconds, representing the highest-frequency ground-based VLBI fringe detection reported to date.
A short-lived fringe detection on the ALMA–APEX baseline confirms that near-terahertz VLBI is technically feasible under excellent weather conditions.

claims.hypothesis: The non-detection of 690 GHz fringes on the intercontinental ALMA-JCMT baseline is due to frequency-dependent coherence and sensitivity losses rather than gross instrumental failure, timing errors, or station clock instability.
claims.experiment: Correlated 230 GHz benchmark scans on the ALMA-JCMT baseline, verified JCMT Band 9 tuning via Orion BN CO(6-5) and telluric H2O spectra, evaluated optical clock Allan variance, and compared predicted vs. measured Band 9 SNRs.
claims.result: Band 6 scans yielded strong fringes (SNR up to 123.3) with aligned clocks/rates; JCMT detected CO(6-5) at 691.435 GHz; clock coherence at 10 s is 0.96 (coherence time 150 s); applying the 40% SNR shortfall seen on ALMA-APEX reduces the predicted ALMA-JCMT SNR of 9 below the detection threshold of ~7.
claims.finding: The ALMA-JCMT non-detection is explained by atmospheric decoherence, finite APS phasing cadence (16 s), and frequency-dependent losses rather than instrumental or clock failure.

evidence.quote: On the ALMA–APEX baseline, the measured SNR was ∼12, above the threshold but 40% below our estimate of 20. This shortfall indicates additional loss terms not captured in the nominal sensitivity estimate. Applying a comparable degradation to the ALMA–JCMT baseline would place its effective SNR below the detection threshold.
Comparison with 230 GHz performance demonstrates that this non-detection is unlikely to result from gross instrumental failure, delay-model errors, or fundamental station instability.

claims.hypothesis: The ALMA Phasing System (APS) with the new delay-fix upgrade can sustain stable phased-array operation at Band 9 across standard 300 s VLBI scans.
claims.experiment: Operated APS at Band 9 on J0423-0120 (~2.3 Jy) and J0433+0521 across four 300 s scans while monitoring near-real-time phasing efficiency.
claims.result: Phasing efficiency on J0423-0120 began at ~70% or better but degraded to ~30% after 1-2 minutes, and never phased well on the weaker target J0433+0521, whereas 230 GHz scans maintained >90% efficiency over 300 s.
claims.finding: APS Band 9 phasing works initially on bright sources under excellent weather but degrades after ~1-2 minutes due to rapid atmospheric fluctuations, dispersive dry-air effects, and the 16 s slow-loop cadence.

evidence.quote: suggests that the APS could only sustain coherent phasing for about one minute before losing effective phase summation.

For the first two scans on the primary targets, the phasing efficiency initially started reasonably well, as expected due to the excellent weather conditions, but subsequently degraded towards a level of 30%.

why_this_data.value: Observations were triggered on 2024 November 21 when weather was simultaneously excellent at Chajnantor (PWV 0.46 mm) and Maunakea (PWV 1.3 mm); J0423-0120 was selected as a bright (~2.3 Jy), compact Band 9 calibrator observable above 30 deg elevation at both sites, Orion BN was chosen to verify CO(6-5) spectral tuning, and a 230 GHz session was included as a system benchmark.

evidence.quote: Both are relatively bright in submillimeter wavelengths and are located such that they could be observed from both ALMA/APEX and JCMT at elevations exceeding 30°, ensuring favorable atmospheric transmission.
In addition, the Becklin–Neugebauer (BN) object in Orion (ORIBN) was selected for dedicated scans to verify the Band 9 spectral-line tuning.
For the primary and secondary targets, we also scheduled a Band 6 (230 GHz) session as a VLBI benchmark test of overall system, since observations in this band are well established.

why_this_method.value: Used the new full-band delay-fix mechanism in APS to reduce residual delay errors across the 2 GHz baseband, disabled 90-deg Walsh switching so the recorded VLBI sum signal was not scrambled, and used segmented incoherent averaging (cohfit) to recover fringe SNR when atmospheric phase fluctuations limit coherent integration.

evidence.quote: To mitigate these challenges, a new phasing mechanism called the delay-fix was introduced—an upgrade that directly measures and corrects delays across the full 2 GHz baseband, replacing the earlier chunked (∼234 MHz) correction scheme.
The purpose of the APS is to provide a combined, coherent signal for recording, and the 90° Walsh-switching process completely scrambles the signal that is ultimately recorded.
is more consistent with the segmented, incoherent-averaging approach used in cohfit, in which fringe strength can still be accumulated when residual phase fluctuations limit fully coherent averaging

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Standard ALMA Band 9 90-degree Walsh phase-switching for DSB-to-SSB separation was rejected/disabled because it occurs outside the APS domain and scrambles the recorded VLBI signal.

evidence.quote: The purpose of the APS is to provide a combined, coherent signal for recording, and the 90° Walsh-switching process completely scrambles the signal that is ultimately recorded. Thus, during the APS operation, the 90° Walsh-switching must be turned off, and the DSB-to-SSB signal conversion is also disabled.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Adopting the ALMA-APEX 20 s solution interval for the ALMA-JCMT baseline was rejected because ALMA and APEX are separated by only a few km and share partially correlated atmospheric fluctuations; instead, the 230 GHz ALMA-JCMT solution interval (30 s) was scaled inversely with frequency to 10 s.

evidence.quote: Because the two sites are separated by only a few kilometers, atmospheric phase fluctuations sampled by the two stations may remain partially correlated (Matsushita et al. 2017b).
Rather than directly adopting the ALMA–APEX value, we use the 230 GHz ALMA–JCMT data as the empirical reference because they sample the same long baseline under similar observing conditions.

how_they_decided_enough.value: Required a minimum SNR of ~7 for robust VLBI fringe detection alongside low probability of false detection (PFD) and physical consistency of delay and rate solutions across polarizations and adjacent scans.

evidence.quote: This classification is based not solely on statistical significance, but also on the physical consistency of the fringe solution, including stability of the delay–rate peak across parallel-hand polarizations and comparison between adjacent scans.
In VLBI practice, a SNR ratio of about ∼7 is generally taken as the minimum for robust fringes (TMS).

limitations_admitted.value: The present dataset does not allow a clean separation of the new delay-fix performance from other contributing factors.

evidence.quote: However, as will be shown in the next sections, the APS performance remained limited by signal-to-noise constraints at these frequencies, and the present dataset does not allow a clean separation of delay-fix performance from other contributing factors.

limitations_admitted.value: APS phasing efficiency at Band 9 degraded after ~1-2 minutes toward ~30%, limiting usable scan durations to ~60-90 s.

evidence.quote: The similar pattern in all the scans suggests that the APS could only sustain coherent phasing for about one minute before losing effective phase summation.

limitations_admitted.value: Adverse weather at the Greenland Telescope (GLT) prevented usable data acquisition there, and a 40 s late recording start at APEX in Scan 1 plus missing polarization channels/data-quality issues in Scan 3 left Scan 2 as the sole robust Band 9 fringe detection.

evidence.quote: However, adverse weather conditions at the GLT site prevented usable data acquisition; no instrumental issues were identified.
recording roughly 40 s late, leaving too little usable overlap for a stable fringe. Scan 3 also produced no detection, consistent with its known data-quality issues and missing polarization channels.

limitations_admitted.value: No dedicated VLBI amplitude calibration scans were obtained due to limited ALMA time, and single linear polarization recording without quarter-wave plates or PolConvert introduced up to a 29% (cos 45 deg ≈ 0.71) amplitude loss.

evidence.quote: Due to the limited allotted ALMA time allocated to this experiment, no dedicated calibration scans were included.

In this experiment, all three stations recorded a single linear polarization. In the worst case, an unknown relative polarization angle can reduce the correlated amplitude by a factor of cos 45° ≈ 0.71, corresponding to a conservative ≈29% loss in correlated flux.

referee_caveats_inferred: Noticeable numerical inconsistency in the source size lower limit for J0423-0120 between Section 7 (≳ 2.6 μas) and Section 8 Summary (≳ 4 μas).
The detected 690 GHz fringe is exclusively on a short (~2 km, 6 Mλ) baseline sharing the same Chajnantor atmosphere, so intercontinental 690 GHz VLBI fringe detection remains unproven.

evidence.quote: The data made available at the ALMA Archive includes a small sample of the recorded VLBI data to allow further investigations of this unique data set.
